items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: ‘That’s Why I’m Not Scared of Death’: NBA Player Michael Porter Jr. Spent a Livestream Telling N3on Jesus Is the Only Way
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Michael Porter Jr. didn’t go on N3on’s stream to talk about God. Then the streamer brought up AI, and the conversation went somewhere else entirely. Porter, who led the Brooklyn Nets in scoring last season at a career-high 24.2 points a game, sat in on Mikyle Rafiq’s Kick livestrea
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Michael Porter Jr. didn’t go on N3on’s stream to talk about God. Then the streamer brought up AI, and the conversation went somewhere else entirely.

Porter, who led the Brooklyn Nets in scoring last season at a career-high 24.2 points a game, sat in on Mikyle Rafiq’s Kick livestream for the better part of Tuesday. Rafiq, who streams as N3on and has more than a million followers on both YouTube and Instagram, said he was worried about where AI is headed. Porter’s answer skipped the technology.

“The world’s just, it’s evil, bro,” he said. “That’s why just make sure you’re right with God, man. Not just any God. Make sure you’re right with Jesus Christ.”

Rafiq said he’s Muslim, respects every religion and tells his viewers to pray to one God. Porter asked what happens if they’re praying to the wrong one.

“But everyone worships the same God, no?” Rafiq said.

“No,” Porter said.

He kept going. “Some people think that the best thing about this life is partying. Some people think the best part about this life is going on a walk with friends. Whatever you think that the point of this life is, there’s gotta be something better than this.”

Then he turned it around. “Are you scared of death?”

“I’m so scared of death,” Rafiq said. “That’s my number one fear.”

Porter told him about a Muslim Uber driver he once asked how he knew he was going to heaven. “He was like, ‘None of us do. We just try to live our best and be a good person, and then we’re all scared, and then we die, and we cross our fingers.'”

“Christianity’s the only religion where it’s like none of us can be good enough to go to heaven, ’cause we’ve all sinned. We’ve all done bad things, and someone else came and died for us and forgave us of our sins. That’s why I’m so secure in the fact that I’m going to heaven, and that’s why I’m not scared of death.”

“Someone else did it for me. Jesus died on the cross for us, dog.”

A few minutes later he invited Rafiq to come to church with him.

Porter has never been quiet about this. He grew up in a devout family in Missouri, won a title with the Nuggets in 2023 and was traded to Brooklyn last summer, where he became the Nets’ best player.

The stream ran almost six hours. This was the part people clipped.

items.title: The Holy Face of Manoppello: Beauty, Strangeness, and Evangelization
items.author: Daniel Fitzpatrick
items.summary:
Daniel Fitzpatrick

If to encounter Christ is at certain moments to be put perfectly at ease, it is at others to be left uncertain of almost everything except that he is Lord.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Daniel Fitzpatrick

I spent the spring of 2011 at the University of Dallas’s Due Santi campus, so called for a well where Sts. Peter and Paul once stopped for a drink. Today, the well sits in the midst of a vineyard, and it’s not hard to imagine the keepers of the sword and the keys leaning there a moment in the evening sunshine glinting off the Tyrrhenian Sea, with Mount Albano gazing down on them and the Appia Antica a few yards off, waiting to bear them the last twelve miles into Rome. The texture of life in those months seemed at once thicker and more diaphanous than usual. Every inch of Italy bore witness to the passage of some saint or sage, and their bones and their relics rose up all round. With grim love I gazed on St. Catherine of Siena’s head. I saw the chains of Paul, Peter’s bones. I climbed the Scala Santa, brought over from the Holy Land by St. Helena. I looked up at Keats’s window and stood before his grave. I longed to touch Bernini’s Pluto and Apollo. I seemed to hear the voices of Ignatius and Francis Xavier and Philip Neri. I stood in Santa Maria Maggiore, whose form Our Lady outlined in the August snow, where Christ’s crèche glows all golden beneath the altar. 

Is it possible to count the relics of Rome? To number the miraculous sights, sacred and profane? To catalogue the crutches left at altars in thanks for miracles? There the things of the world seem all to have been touched with divinity till the whole fabric of reality shimmers, intimating a world impossibly bigger and more lively than we know. So it seemed to me—or seems in these memories which have become my life—that life has been shaped by miracles, by relics, by the saints.

Just after my tenth birthday, my mother enjoyed an apparently miraculous healing through the intercession of Bl. Francis Xavier Seelos after a stroke left the right side of her body paralyzed. The morning after our pastor brought her Bl. Seelos’s relic, my father hung it around her neck and left her to watch Mass on television in her hospital room. At the final blessing, she tried to make the Sign of the Cross and found that her hand and arm worked again. She rose from bed and played the Ode to Joy on a therapy keyboard in the corner. She was healed.

Still, I confess that after a certain point, the reliquary torrent of my Rome semester evoked a touch of skepticism. Isn’t it all too much? I wondered. Is it really so likely those bedazzled sticks of sycamore could be the manger of the Christ? I said as much to a classmate one evening in the mensa over pasta and bread and oil. This was a fellow of great zeal—particularly where fun was concerned—intense appetite, not least with respect to the juice of the grape and the grain, and stentorian voice, now directed full blast against me.

“Why wouldn’t you believe it anyway?” he said.

I dithered half-heartedly. 

“Why wouldn’t you want something good that’s offered to you?” he went on.

In the moment, a dozen arguments occurred to me, as they occur to me still, yet in such cases, reason often matters rather little. A voice within said, “He’s right, you know.” And whatever else might be said on the matter, my friend’s words reframed the way I met the many wonders that would continue to greet me that semester. I was the better and the happier, and I was all the more ready for an encounter that would come in the middle of spring with the face of Christ.

A classmate, having read of il Volto Santo di Manoppello, the veil bearing a miraculous image of the face of the Crucified and Risen Christ, arranged a class visit thereto. A charter bus bore us out early one morning from beneath the umbrella pines, and as the sun came up out of the far Adriatic, we made across the spine of the Apennines for the town—modest by Italian standards—of Manoppello. We arrived, we processed into the church, we trooped around to the shrine at the back of the altar and knelt and prayed, or stood and wept, or gazed a moment and went on back into the spring sunshine, back to the bus, back to Rome. 

I was encouraged to keep a journal that semester and did so. It sits high in a closet, and I pull it down from time to time and console myself—it’s a funny little artifact, full of high sentences and a bit obtuse. Beneath the heading “Manoppello” lies a lone sentence—the quarter-inch gravestone of that day—“I have just seen the face of God.” Several blank pages follow. No doubt I meant to wax away, and perhaps that bare space was merely the portal to the present musings. 

What I did not set down during all the bus ride back to Due Santi was how deeply the face of God had unsettled me. If to encounter Christ is at certain moments to be put perfectly at ease, it is at others to be left uncertain of almost everything except that he is Lord. The latter feeling haunted me like the very sun that tracked our passage toward the coast and settled down ahead of us on the horizon and plunged into the sea as the bus eased beneath the sheltering pines of campus. Christ’s face seemed to loom up in the dark, confronting me in the midst of what I had to that time called beauty—what I still see as the beauty of Michelangelo’s sculpture, Waugh’s prose, Velasquez’s painting—calling me to the little lower layer, as Ahab puts it. For the face I met behind the altar in Manopello, the face Padre Pio apparently sat before by means of bilocation on the day of his death, was not a face I would at first call beautiful, “so marred was his appearance, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of mortals” (Is 52:14). Nor was the strangeness of that face a mere function of the marks of Christ’s passion. Even beneath the blows and the bruises, below the blood and spittle, the face was plain. The man who gazed at me was not one who would have called me to follow him by the compulsion of the beauty the eye finds unassisted.

Yet Christ is the beautiful one. Beauty, St. Thomas tells us, is “quod visum placet,” that which, having been seen, pleases. The beauty of the face of Manoppello, the beauty of the Crucified Christ, serves as a reminder that the way of beauty is not automatic, that the perception of the most beautiful things does not rely simply on the senses but on the harmony between the senses and the intellect, and that this harmonization takes time and effort and good counsel. St. Peter’s Basilica may compel my wonder, but it takes, for some of us, a lifetime’s discipline to enter upon the awareness of Christ’s beauty as it appears to us on the altar of the humblest country church, in the tabernacle of a lowly chapel, in the bruised body oozing on the tree of the cross. 

That face comes frequently to me now as I consider, as a teacher, as a writer, as a father, as one struggling along in search of the Way, how to evangelize. The numbers, it would seem, are against us. Here and there may shine some spark of revival, but on the whole, the tale of declining church attendance, of disbelief in Christ’s real presence, of disaffiliation with religion, lies open for the reading in graph after graph after graph. Those statistics are surely important. They should not go ignored. Yet I can’t help feeling—with something of the feeling of that strange face in Manoppello—that to frame our efforts at evangelization in terms of the statistics is in some way to miss the mark. Post after post on social media suggests that if we could just get it right, if we could just build the right way, decorate the right way, preach the right way, faith would necessarily follow. But the Gospels are themselves frequently catalogues of revelation rejected. Christ calls the crowds to eat his flesh. They turn away. He reprimands their fickle hearts. They seek to kill him. He is lifted up upon the cross. They scatter. The Word himself bears witness to the light, and we choose instead the darkness.

“Quantitative judgments don’t apply” in matters of the spiritual life, says Peregrine Crouchback in Evelyn Waugh’s Sword of Honor trilogy. With due respect to the statistics, I nonetheless submit, in light of the Holy Face of Manoppello, that where faith is concerned, it’s the anecdote that counts, the moment of contact with the Christ which from then on orders all other moments, the need to tell others and to seek him in every crease and wrinkle of creation. Our minds find comfort in abstraction. Il Volto Santo recalls us to the deep, to the shaking that keeps us steady.

We love to repeat, with Prince Myshkin, that beauty will save the world. But we know better. We know that beauty has already saved the world and that he continues his labor of salvation moment by moment. We ought, by all means, to build beautiful churches, to learn to preach the good news with every ounce of art at our disposal, to shape what lies within our purview to adumbrate the loveliness of Christ, remembering, though, that his loveliness is often at work in secret, that glory shines forth in the stripes of his affliction, that even he watched the crowds get up and shake their heads and walk away. 

He has already saved the world. Bruised, he gazes still, gleaming in secret, inviting us to be recalled to life. 

A version of this essay appears in The Wheel and the Clay: The Inner Lives of Christian Artists, launching September 30 from Ignatius Press and featuring essays by Sally Read, Dana Gioia, James Matthew Wilson, Arvo Part, and others.

items.title: Saturday, September 19, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus explains the purpose of the parables: “Knowledge of the mysteries of the Kingdom of God has been granted to you;
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 15:35-37, 42-49

But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” Fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare seed, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.

So it is with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power. It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a physical body, there is also a spiritual body. Thus it is written, “The first man, Adam, became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first, but the physical, and then the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so are those who are of the dust; and as is the man of heaven, so are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we will also bear the image of the man of heaven.

Psalm
Psalm 56:10c-12, 13-14

  In God, whose word I praise,
    in the Lord, whose word I praise,
in God I trust; I am not afraid.
    What can a mere mortal do to me?
My vows to you I must perform, O God;
    I will render thank offerings to you.
For you have delivered my soul from death,
    and my feet from falling,
so that I may walk before God
    in the light of life.

Gospel Reading
Luke 8:4-15

When a great crowd gathered and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: “A sower went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell on the path and was trampled on, and the birds of the air ate it up. Some fell on the rock; and as it grew up, it withered for lack of moisture. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew with it and choked it. Some fell into good soil, and when it grew, it produced a hundredfold.” As he said this, he called out, “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”

Then his disciples asked him what this parable meant. He said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God; but to others I speak in parables, so that

‘looking they may not perceive,
    and listening they may not understand.’

“Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones on the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe only for a while and in a time of testing fall away. As for what fell among the thorns, these are the ones who hear; but as they go on their way, they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. But as for that in the good soil, these are the ones who, when they hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus explains the purpose of the parables: “Knowledge of the mysteries of the Kingdom of God has been granted to you; but to the rest, they are made known through parables so that they may look but not see, and hear but not understand.”

The use of the word “para” in the New Testament signals the failure to see at various levels. The great metaphor here is the blindness of the Jews, a blindness that is identified with disobedience.

The parables of Christ are meant to highlight and point out this blindness, this willful refusal to see. They themselves, in their peculiar form, are judgments on those who cannot see in them signs of salvation.

The parables are often exercises whose purpose is to confuse and confound the hearer, overturning her expectations and upsetting her theological convictions. A parable does its work by turning our ordinary conception of the spiritual world upside down. And we would be greatly remiss if we did not attend to the instruction that emerges from those startling, funny, off-putting, and strangely enlightening stories that Jesus loved to tell.
